theorem.cauchy.hypothesis.0: Both f and g are continuous on [a, b].
theorem.cauchy.hypothesis.2: $g'(x) \neq 0$ on $(a, b)$, which also gives $g(b) \neq g(a)$.
theorem.cauchy.pitfall.0: Taking g(x) = x recovers the ordinary Mean Value Theorem.
theorem.cauchy.pitfall.1: The condition on g is what prevents division by zero in the conclusion.
theorem.cauchy.pitfall.2: Cauchy's theorem is the tool behind L'Hôpital's rule.
theorem.cauchy.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $g'(x) \neq 0$ on $(a, b)$, then there exists $c$ in $(a, b)$ with $f'(c)/g'(c)$ equal to $(f(b) - f(a)) / (g(b) - g(a))$.
theorem.cauchy.title: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem
theorem.cauchy.why: It compares the two functions through a common parameter: each is a curve, and the theorem locates a point where their tangent directions match the overall change.
theorem.darboux.hypothesis.0: f is differentiable on the interval.
theorem.darboux.pitfall.0: The derivative need not be continuous, so the ordinary IVT does not apply to it directly.
theorem.darboux.statement: If $f$ is differentiable on an interval, then $f'$ has the intermediate value property there: it takes every value between any two of its values.
theorem.darboux.title: Darboux's theorem
theorem.darboux.why: Derivatives cannot jump, even though they need not be continuous; this is a surprising and useful rigidity property.
theorem.differentiable_implies_continuou: f(x) = |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0.
A vertical tangent gives an infinite slope and therefore no derivative.
If f is differentiable at c, then f is continuous at c. The converse fails: continuity does not imply differentiability.
A finite slope forces the graph to close up into a single unbroken point, so a jump or a hole is impossible wherever a derivative exists.
theorem.differentiation_rules.hypothesis: Each rule needs the relevant derivatives to exist.
The inverse rule needs $f'(a) \neq 0$ at the point.
theorem.differentiation_rules.pitfall.0: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.
theorem.differentiation_rules.pitfall.1: The chain rule leaves the inner function intact as a factor.
theorem.differentiation_rules.pitfall.2: The inverse rule gives the reciprocal slope, not the inverse of the function value.
theorem.differentiation_rules.statement: Product, quotient, chain and inverse function rules, stated as the algebra that turns the derivatives of the pieces into the derivative of the whole.
theorem.differentiation_rules.title: The differentiation rules
theorem.differentiation_rules.why: Differentiation is linear plus a small set of structural rules; every derivative is built by combining them.
theorem.evt.hypothesis.0: The interval is closed and bounded.
theorem.evt.hypothesis.1: f is continuous on the whole interval.
theorem.evt.pitfall.0: Both assumptions matter: f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] and f(x) = x on (0, 1) both fail.
theorem.evt.pitfall.1: It guarantees the extremes exist; finding them still needs the critical-point work.
theorem.evt.statement: If f is continuous on a closed bounded interval [a, b], then f attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval.
theorem.evt.title: Extreme Value Theorem (Weierstrass)
theorem.evt.why: A continuous curve on a finite closed interval cannot escape to infinity or sneak past an endpoint, so it must reach its highest and lowest values.
theorem.fermat.hypothesis.0: c is an interior point of the domain.
theorem.fermat.hypothesis.1: f has a local extremum at c.
theorem.fermat.pitfall.0: The converse is false: $f'(c) = 0$ does not guarantee an extremum (consider $f(x) = x^3$ at $0$).
theorem.fermat.pitfall.1: The point must be interior; an endpoint can be an extremum without $f'$ being zero.
theorem.fermat.statement: If $f$ has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point $c$ of its domain and $f$ is differentiable there, then $f'(c) = 0$.
theorem.fermat.title: Fermat's theorem
theorem.fermat.why: At a smooth peak or trough the tangent flattens out, so the instantaneous rate of change must be zero.
theorem.first_derivative_test.hypothesis: c is a critical point of f.
f is continuous at c and differentiable on a punctured neighbourhood of it.
theorem.first_derivative_test.pitfall.0: The test needs a genuine sign change on both sides, not just $f'(c) = 0$.
theorem.first_derivative_test.pitfall.1: If $f'$ does not change sign, the point is a stationary turning point rather than an extremum.
theorem.first_derivative_test.statement: At a critical point $c$: if $f'$ changes from positive to negative, $c$ is a local maximum; if it changes from negative to positive, $c$ is a local minimum; if it keeps its sign, $c$ is neither.
theorem.first_derivative_test.title: First derivative test
theorem.first_derivative_test.why: The function switches from climbing to falling exactly at a maximum and the reverse at a minimum, so the sign change is the decisive evidence.
theorem.inflection.pitfall.0: $f''(c) = 0$ alone is not enough; an actual sign change is required.
theorem.inflection.pitfall.1: $f(x) = x^4$ has $f''(0) = 0$ but no inflection at the origin.
theorem.inflection.statement: If $f''$ exists and changes sign at $c$, then $(c, f(c))$ is an inflection point and the concavity of $f$ flips there.
theorem.inflection.title: Inflection point criterion
theorem.inflection.why: Concavity describes which way the curve bends; when the bending direction flips, the curve has an inflection point.
theorem.lhopital.hypothesis.0: The quotient is an indeterminate form $0/0$ or $\pm\infty/\pm\infty$ at $a$.
theorem.lhopital.hypothesis.1: $f$ and $g$ are differentiable near $a$, with $g'(x) \neq 0$ there.
theorem.lhopital.hypothesis.2: The limit of $f'/g'$ exists (or is infinite).
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.0: Never apply it before verifying the form really is indeterminate.
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.1: The rule applies to the quotient as a whole, not to products or sums term by term.
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.2: For $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty-\infty$, $1^\infty$, $0^0$ and $\infty^0$, rewrite the expression into a $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ quotient first.
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.3: If the new limit is worse, stop: the rule gave no information.
theorem.lhopital.statement: If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable near $a$ and both tend to $0$ or both tend to $\pm\infty$ at $a$, and the limit of $f'(x)/g'(x)$ exists, then the limit of $f(x)/g(x)$ equals that same limit.
theorem.lhopital.title: L'Hôpital's rule
theorem.lhopital.why: Near the point the two functions are dominated by their linear behaviour, so comparing their slopes replaces comparing their values.
x is close enough to a for the error to be acceptable.
theorem.linear_approximation.pitfall.0: The approximation degrades quickly away from a.
theorem.linear_approximation.pitfall.1: It is only first order: the error grows like $(x - a)^2$.
theorem.linear_approximation.statement: If $f$ is differentiable at $a$, then for $x$ near $a$ we have $f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$, and the error is small compared with $(x - a)$.
theorem.linear_approximation.title: Linear approximation and the differential
theorem.linear_approximation.why: Zooming in far enough makes any smooth curve look like its tangent line, which is the practical meaning of the derivative.
theorem.monotonicity.hypothesis.0: f is continuous on the interval and differentiable on its interior.
theorem.monotonicity.hypothesis.1: The sign of $f'$ is constant on the interval.
theorem.monotonicity.pitfall.0: The intervals of monotonicity are separated by the critical points of f.
theorem.monotonicity.pitfall.1: A single critical point does not by itself determine the sign on either side.
theorem.monotonicity.statement: If $f'(x) > 0$ on an interval then $f$ is strictly increasing there; if $f'(x) < 0$ then $f$ is strictly decreasing there.
theorem.monotonicity.title: Monotonicity test
theorem.monotonicity.why: A positive slope means the graph climbs as you move right, so the sign of the derivative reads directly as the direction of the function.
theorem.mvt.pitfall.0: Continuity is required on the CLOSED interval and differentiability on the OPEN one.
theorem.mvt.pitfall.1: The theorem promises existence; it does not tell you where until you solve for c.
theorem.mvt.pitfall.2: f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] shows differentiability cannot be dropped.
theorem.mvt.statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, then there exists at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$ such that $f'(c)$ equals the secant slope $(f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a)$.
theorem.mvt.title: Mean Value Theorem (Lagrange)
theorem.mvt.why: Somewhere the instantaneous rate of change must equal the average rate of change over the whole interval, so some tangent is parallel to the secant.
theorem.rolle.hypothesis.0: f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b].
theorem.rolle.hypothesis.1: f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b).
theorem.rolle.pitfall.0: Without f(a) = f(b) the conclusion can fail completely.
theorem.rolle.pitfall.1: Rolle is the special horizontal case of the Mean Value Theorem.
theorem.rolle.statement: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $f(a) = f(b)$, then there exists at least one $c$ in $(a, b)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.
theorem.rolle.title: Rolle's theorem
theorem.rolle.why: If the graph starts and ends at the same height, it must turn around somewhere inside and that turning point has a horizontal tangent.
theorem.second_derivative_test.pitfall.0: When $f''(c) = 0$ nothing is decided; fall back to the first derivative test.
theorem.second_derivative_test.pitfall.1: This test only applies at stationary points, not at endpoints.
theorem.second_derivative_test.statement: If $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''(c) > 0$ then $c$ is a local minimum; if $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''(c) < 0$ then $c$ is a local maximum. If $f''(c) = 0$ the test is inconclusive.
theorem.second_derivative_test.title: Second derivative test
theorem.second_derivative_test.why: Concavity is the tiebreaker: an upward-opening curve at a flat point is a valley, and a downward-opening one is a peak.
theorem.taylor.hypothesis.0: f has n + 1 continuous derivatives on the interval.
theorem.taylor.hypothesis.1: ξ lies strictly between a and x.
theorem.taylor.pitfall.0: The remainder gives an error bound, not the exact error.
theorem.taylor.pitfall.1: The point ξ is guaranteed to exist but is not identified.
theorem.taylor.statement: If $f$ has $n + 1$ derivatives on an interval containing $a$ and $x$, then $f(x)$ equals its degree $n$ Taylor polynomial at $a$ plus a remainder involving $f^{(n+1)}$ at some point between $a$ and $x$.
theorem.taylor.title: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder
theorem.taylor.why: A smooth function is locally indistinguishable from a polynomial, and the remainder measures exactly how good that approximation is.
theorem.zero_derivative.hypothesis.0: The set is a single interval, not a union of separate pieces.
theorem.zero_derivative.hypothesis.1: f is differentiable with zero derivative throughout it.
theorem.zero_derivative.pitfall.0: On a disconnected domain the conclusion can fail piecewise.
theorem.zero_derivative.pitfall.1: This is what justifies writing one arbitrary constant in an indefinite integral.
theorem.zero_derivative.statement: If $f'(x) = 0$ for every $x$ in an interval, then $f$ is constant on that interval.
theorem.zero_derivative.title: Zero derivative implies constant
theorem.zero_derivative.why: Two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant, which is why an antiderivative always carries a + C.

ui.a_closed_interval_leaves_nothing_to_c: A closed interval leaves nothing to chance
ui.a_curve_crosses_the_family_at_the_con: A curve crosses the family at the constant angle $\alpha$ when $\tan\alpha = (m_t - m)/(1 + m_t m)$. Solving for the trajectory slope gives $m_t = (m + \tan\alpha)/(1 - m\tan\alpha)$, the differential equation of the oblique family.
ui.a_definite_integral_adds_up_signed_ar: A definite integral adds up signed area; an indefinite integral lists every antiderivative at once. The two are linked by the fundamental theorem.
ui.a_derivative_is_a_local_rate: A derivative is a local rate
ui.a_first_order_equation_describes_a_wh: A first-order equation describes a whole family of curves. Solving finds the relation that makes the equation true, with one constant C left free until an initial condition fixes it.
ui.a_function_is_continuous_at_a_point_w: A function is continuous at a point when it is defined there, its two-sided limit exists, and that limit equals the function value. All three must hold together.
A function is continuous at a point when the left limit and the right limit exist, are equal, and equal the value of the function.
ui.a_horizontal_family_has_slope_0_the_o: A horizontal family has slope $0$; the oblique trajectory slope is $\tan\alpha = 1$.
ui.a_horizontal_tangent_has_a_vertical_n: A horizontal tangent has a vertical normal, whose slope does not exist.
ui.a_partial_derivative_treats_every_oth: A partial derivative treats every other variable as a constant. The gradient collects the first partials into one vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase.
ui.a_relation_such_as_x_y_25_describes_a: A relation such as $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ describes a shape, but if a point moves along it then $x$ and $y$ both depend on time. Differentiating the whole relation with respect to $t$ applies the chain rule to each quantity and leaves an equation linking their rates.
ui.a_removable_gap_can_be_repaired_by_re: A removable gap can be repaired by redefining one point; a jump or an infinite break cannot.
ui.a_removable_hole_belongs_to_neither_t: A removable hole belongs to neither the domain nor the range at that exact value, even though the limit there exists.
ui.a_series_is_a_sequence_of_partial_sum: A series is a sequence of partial sums. Convergence means those sums approach a limit; the tests are shortcuts that prove this without computing every sum.
ui.a_sign_change_of_f_from_to_is_a_local: A sign change of $f'$ from $+$ to $-$ is a local maximum, and from $-$ to $+$ is a local minimum.
ui.a_sign_change_of_f_marks_an_inflectio: A sign change of $f''$ marks an inflection point, where concavity flips.
ui.a_stationary_turning_point_such_as_x_: A stationary turning point such as $x = 0$ for $x^3$ has $f' = 0$ but is neither a maximum nor a minimum.
ui.a_term_that_tends_to_0_is_necessary_b: A term that tends to 0 is necessary but not sufficient: 1/n tends to 0 while its series diverges.
ui.a_unique_solution_passes_through_this: Both $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous at this point, so a unique solution passes through it.
ui.a_vertical_tangent_has_no_finite_slop: A vertical tangent has no finite slope. The solver treats that case separately instead of dividing by zero.
ui.a_zero_wronskian_at_a_single_point_do: A zero Wronskian at a single point does not by itself prove dependence for arbitrary functions.
ui.alternating_if_a_n_decreases_to_0_the: Alternating: if |a_n| decreases to 0, the series converges (possibly conditionally).
ui.an_envelope_is_a_curve_tangent_to_eve: An envelope is a curve tangent to every member of a family. Orthogonal trajectories are the family that crosses every member at a right angle.
ui.an_existing_limit_is_not_enough_the_v: An existing limit is not enough: the value f(a) must also be defined and match it.
ui.an_indefinite_integral_without_c_is_i: An indefinite integral without + C is incomplete, and bounds must follow the same order as the differentials.
ui.approximate_a_function_by_a_polynomia: Approximate a function by a polynomial built from its derivatives at one point.
ui.area_between_curves_volume_of_revolut: Area between curves, volume of revolution and arc length, with the integral set up and evaluated.
ui.area_integrate_f_g_splitting_at_the_i: Area: integrate |f − g|, splitting at the intersection points.
ui.at_90_the_formula_reduces_to_y_1_y_th: At α = 90° the formula reduces to y′ = −1/y′, the orthogonal family.
ui.at_the_chosen_instant_the_relation_be: At the chosen instant the relation behaves locally like a line through the marked point, and that line slope is the ratio of the two rates.

ui.the_definite_integral_is_the_signed_a: The definite integral is the signed area between this curve and the x-axis, accumulated from the lower to the upper bound.
ui.the_derivative_evaluated_at_a_gives_t: The derivative evaluated at a gives the slope of the tangent. The normal is the line through the same point whose slope is the negative reciprocal, because perpendicular slopes multiply to -1.
ui.the_derivative_is_the_slope_of_the_or: The derivative is the slope of the original curve. Where f′ crosses zero the tangent is horizontal.
ui.the_derivative_is_the_slope_of_the_ta: The derivative is the slope of the tangent line: how fast the output changes for a tiny change in the input. Higher orders repeat that idea on the previous derivative.
ui.the_derivative_of_a_product_is_not_th: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.
ui.the_determinant_never_vanishes_so_the: The determinant never vanishes, so the two exponentials are independent on every interval.

step.hint.apply_the_boundary_conditions: Only modes that vanish at both ends survive; every other coefficient is forced to zero.
step.hint.build_the_characteristic_polyn: Collect the coefficients of x^r; the roots r decide which of the three solution shapes applies.
step.hint.build_the_fundamental_matrix: The columns are independent solutions, so the matrix carries the initial vector to time t.
step.hint.build_the_partial_sum: Truncate the series after N terms; the omitted tail is exactly the error being estimated.
step.hint.build_the_polynomial: Expand the recurrence explicitly so the polynomial can be evaluated at any point.
step.hint.check_orthogonality_and_parsev: The same two checks as in Fourier series: orthogonality of the modes and conservation of energy.
step.hint.check_parseval_and_the_boundar: Parseval compares the energy of $f$ with the energy of the partial sum; the boundary value must also vanish.
step.hint.check_the_coefficients: Self-adjoint form needs p > 0 and w > 0 on the open interval; otherwise the eigenproblem is singular.
step.hint.check_the_conserved_quantity: The wave energy stays constant in time; a numerical drift is evidence of a bad step size.
step.hint.check_the_ode_and_orthogonalit: Verify that the sampled eigenfunctions solve the ODE and are orthogonal under the stated weight.
step.hint.check_the_rayleigh_quotient: The Rayleigh quotient must reproduce every computed eigenvalue; a mismatch means the grid is too coarse.
step.hint.check_transversality_and_stabi: Orbits must cross the section in one direction, and nearby orbits must approach the same closed curve.
step.hint.choose_the_expansion_point: The series is built around x0, and its radius of convergence reaches the nearest singular point.
step.hint.choose_the_orthogonal_family: The interval and the weight select the family: Legendre, Chebyshev, sine, cosine or Bessel.
step.hint.classify_each_equilibrium: The trace and determinant of the Jacobian at each equilibrium name its local behaviour.
step.hint.classify_the_linearization: Trace, determinant and discriminant together name the local phase portrait.
step.hint.collect_equal_powers: Shift the indices until every term carries the same power, then compare coefficients term by term.
step.hint.compare_with_the_nonlinear_fie: Close to the equilibrium the linear and nonlinear pictures must agree; far away they may differ.
step.hint.compute_the_coefficients: Each coefficient is the inner product of f with its basis function, divided by the mode's norm.
step.hint.compute_the_fourier_coefficien: Orthogonality isolates one mode at a time: project f onto it and divide by the norm squared.
step.hint.compute_the_indicial_equation: Substituting the Frobenius series into the ODE leaves the lowest power of x, whose coefficient gives r.
step.hint.compute_the_jacobian: Linearizing at an equilibrium replaces the vector field by its Jacobian at that point.
step.hint.compute_the_jacobian_at_each_p: Every equilibrium gets its own Jacobian, so the same system can behave differently at each one.
step.hint.compute_the_pole_orders: A regular singular point needs (x - x0) p and (x - x0)^2 q to stay finite as x approaches x0.
step.hint.conclude_from_the_sign: $V' < 0$ strictly gives asymptotic stability; $V' \le 0$ alone gives only stability.
step.hint.conclusion: Collect the earlier steps into one statement about what the solution does.
step.hint.diagonalize_or_use_the_spectra: Diagonalizing turns the matrix exponential into scalar exponentials on the diagonal.
step.hint.differentiate_along_the_flow: $V' = \nabla V \cdot (f, g)$ measures how the candidate changes along the orbits.
step.hint.discretize_the_interval: Replace the derivatives with finite differences on a grid of N + 1 points.
step.hint.discretize_with_finite_differe: A symmetric difference matrix keeps the discrete problem self-adjoint.
step.hint.divide_by_the_eigenvalue: Each mode is scaled by 1/(lambda_n - q); a zero denominator means the forcing is in resonance.
step.hint.estimate_the_convergence_order: Halving the step should cut the error by a factor 2^p; the measured slope is p.
step.hint.estimate_the_error: Compare the solution at two step sizes; their difference estimates the local error.
step.hint.estimate_the_lyapunov_exponent: Separate two nearby orbits and measure how fast their distance grows exponentially.
step.hint.estimate_the_period: The time between successive crossings of a section gives the period of the cycle.
step.hint.evaluate: Substitute the requested time into the closed form to turn it into a number.
step.hint.evaluate_at_the_point: Insert the point into the polynomial; the second-kind function is added only when asked for.
step.hint.evaluate_the_amount: Set t to the requested time to get the amount or concentration at that moment.
step.hint.evaluate_the_integral: Apply the chosen technique, then differentiate the answer to check it.
step.hint.evaluate_the_series: Sum enough terms for the requested accuracy; the terms decay factorially.
step.hint.expand_the_forcing: Write the forcing in the eigenfunctions of the homogeneous problem; the coefficients are inner products.
step.hint.find_the_bessel_zeros: A Bessel series uses the zeros of J_nu, not multiples of pi.
step.hint.find_the_characteristic_curves: For constant coefficients the characteristics are straight lines; their direction classifies the PDE.
step.hint.find_the_characteristic_polyno: $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ packs all the eigenvalues into one polynomial.
step.hint.find_the_equilibria: Equilibria solve $f = g = 0$; only the ones inside the chosen window are reported.
step.hint.first_frobenius_series: The larger indicial root gives one series; its coefficients follow the recurrence.
step.hint.function_and_derivatives: Differentiate repeatedly at the centre until the requested degree is reached.
step.hint.identify_the_singular_endpoint: A zero of p at an endpoint makes the problem singular; the boundary condition is then implicit.
step.hint.integrate_the_planar_system: Follow the orbit numerically until it settles on a closed curve.
step.hint.linearize_at_the_equilibrium: Shift the origin to the equilibrium and keep only the linear terms.
step.hint.measure_the_convergence_order: The error should decay like $1/N^p$; the slope on a log-log plot measures $p$.
step.hint.numeric_evidence: The table samples the computed object so the result can be checked numerically, not only symbolically.
step.hint.report_the_weight_and_boundary: State the weight and how the eigenfunctions behave at the singular end.
step.hint.second_frobenius_series: The smaller root gives the second series; if the roots differ by an integer a logarithm may appear.
step.hint.second_solution: When the indicial roots differ by an integer, the second solution needs a logarithm or a second-kind function.
step.hint.separate_the_variables: A product $u = X(x)\,T(t)$ splits the PDE into two ordinary differential equations.
step.hint.solve_the_associated_eigenvalu: Expand the forcing in the eigenfunctions of the homogeneous problem, then solve mode by mode.
step.hint.solve_the_characteristic_equat: The characteristics are the curves along which the PDE reduces to an ODE.
step.hint.solve_the_generalized_eigenpro: The weight $w$ turns the eigenproblem into the generalized form $Av = \lambda Bv$.
step.hint.solve_the_linear_equation: The tank model is linear in Q, so an integrating factor gives Q(t) directly.
step.hint.solve_the_lyapunov_equation: $A^T P + PA = -Q$ with $Q$ positive definite certifies asymptotic stability.
step.hint.solve_the_tridiagonal_system: The matrix is tridiagonal, so a direct elimination solves it in linear time.
step.hint.split_into_real_and_imaginary_: Complex eigenvalues give complex exponentials; Euler's formula turns them into real sines and cosines.
step.hint.state_the_series: Write the partial sum $S_N$ that will be compared with $f$.
step.hint.substitute_the_data: Insert k, the ambient temperature and the initial temperature into Newton's law solution.
step.hint.substitute_y_equals_x_to_the_r: For a Cauchy–Euler equation, $y = x^r$ turns every term into the same power of $x$.
step.hint.use_the_bonnet_recurrence: Bonnet's relation builds P_n from the two previous polynomials.
step.hint.variation_of_parameters: For a nonhomogeneous system, let the constants of the homogeneous solution vary.
step.hint.verify_the_regular_singular_po: Both limits must be finite; otherwise the Frobenius method does not apply.
step.hint.write_p_and_q: Read p and q from standard form before testing the point.
step.hint.write_the_balance_law: Conservation of momentum for a small segment gives the wave equation.
step.hint.write_the_bessel_equation: Bessel's equation appears in cylindrical problems after separating the variables.
step.hint.write_the_candidate: Choose $V$ positive definite, then check the sign of $V'$ along the flow.
step.hint.write_the_canonical_problem: Fix the equation, the domain and the boundary data before choosing a method.
step.hint.write_the_competing_species_sy: Each population grows logistically and loses members to the other species.
step.hint.write_the_equation_in_standard: Divide by the leading coefficient so the series method sees $y'' + p\,y' + q\,y = 0$.
step.hint.write_the_finite_difference_eq: Each interior node gives one linear equation; the boundary values move to the right side.
step.hint.write_the_fourier_definition: A periodic function is a sum of sines and cosines; the integrals give the weights.
step.hint.write_the_frobenius_series: Here the indicial equation has a double root, so one Frobenius series is expected.
step.hint.write_the_general_solution: A linear combination of the basis solutions with arbitrary constants covers every solution.
step.hint.write_the_legendre_equation: Legendre's equation is the theta part of Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates.
step.hint.write_the_matrix: The coefficient matrix is read directly from the system.
step.hint.write_the_model: The physical balance plus the boundary conditions define the PDE problem.

study.la_fields.title: Fields and linear systems
study.la_fields.subtitle: Why division is allowed, and what row reduction really does.
study.la_fields.short_answer: A field is a set where $+$ and $\cdot$ behave like the rationals: every nonzero element has an inverse. The three elementary row operations are invertible, so row-equivalent systems have exactly the same solutions.
study.la_fields.pitfalls: Dividing by a pivot that is zero, and treating a free variable as if it were determined. Over a finite field, adding a row to itself can kill it: in $\mathbb{F}_2$, $1+1=0$.
study.la_fields.key_idea.0: A field has two operations, both associative and commutative, with identities $0$ and $1$, additive inverses, and a multiplicative inverse for every nonzero element.
study.la_fields.key_idea.1: $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ are fields. $\mathbb{Z}$ is not, because $2$ has no inverse in $\mathbb{Z}$.
study.la_fields.key_idea.2: Swapping rows, adding a multiple of one row to another, and scaling a row by a nonzero scalar each have an inverse of the same kind.
study.la_fields.key_idea.3: A homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations always has a nonzero solution.
study.la_fields.theory.0: A field is a set $F$ with two operations $+$ and $\cdot$ such that $F$ is an abelian group under $+$, the nonzero elements form an abelian group under $\cdot$, and multiplication distributes over addition. The identities are written $0$ and $1$.
study.la_fields.theory.1: The one property that separates a field from a commutative ring is the inverse of a nonzero element. That is exactly the property Gaussian elimination needs when it divides by a pivot.
study.la_fields.theory.2: Each elementary row operation is invertible, so the solution set is unchanged. A system is solved by reaching row echelon form and then reading the pivot columns as basic variables and the rest as free variables.
study.la_fields.theory.3: Theorem. If $A$ is $m\times n$ with $m<n$, the homogeneous system $A\mathbf{x}=0$ has a nonzero solution. Proof: there are at most $m$ pivots among $n$ columns, so at least one column is free, and a free variable can be set to $1$.

study.la_vector_spaces.subtitle: Subspaces, spanning sets, independence, and the number that survives a change of basis.
study.la_vector_spaces.short_answer: A vector space is an abelian group with scalar multiplication that distributes over addition. A basis is an independent spanning set, and every basis of a fixed space has the same size: the dimension.
study.la_vector_spaces.pitfalls: Confusing spanning with independence. A spanning set may be dependent, and an independent set may fail to span. In $\mathbb{R}^2$, three vectors are always dependent, and two vectors span only when they are not multiples.
study.la_vector_spaces.key_idea.0: A subspace is nonempty and closed under addition and scalar multiplication; every other axiom is inherited.
study.la_vector_spaces.key_idea.1: A set spans when every vector of the space is a finite linear combination of its elements.
study.la_vector_spaces.key_idea.2: A set is independent when the only combination equal to $0$ has all coefficients zero.
study.la_vector_spaces.key_idea.3: A basis is independent and spanning, and the dimension is the common size of every basis.
study.la_vector_spaces.theory.0: A vector space over a field $F$ is a set $V$ with addition and scalar multiplication such that $V$ is an abelian group under addition and $\alpha(u+v)=\alpha u+\alpha v$, $(\alpha+\beta)v=\alpha v+\beta v$, $(\alpha\beta)v=\alpha(\beta v)$ and $1v=v$.
study.la_vector_spaces.theory.1: A subset $W$ is a subspace exactly when it is nonempty and closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Checking those two closures covers the whole definition.
study.la_vector_spaces.theory.2: The span of a set is the smallest subspace that contains it. A set is independent when no element lies in the span of the others. A basis is a set that is both independent and spanning.
study.la_vector_spaces.theory.3: Theorem. Any two bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same number of elements. The proof exchanges elements one at a time: an independent set can never be larger than a spanning set.
study.la_vector_spaces.theory.4: Coordinates. Once a basis $B=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ is fixed, every vector has exactly one coordinate vector $(c_1,\dots,c_n)$ with $v=\sum c_i b_i$. This uniqueness is the bridge from vector spaces to matrices.

study.la_transformations.title: Linear transformations and matrices
study.la_transformations.subtitle: A matrix is a linear map in coordinates, and composition is multiplication.
study.la_transformations.short_answer: A map is linear when $T(\alpha u+v)=\alpha T(u)+T(v)$. Fixing bases turns it into a matrix, composition becomes multiplication, and rank plus nullity equals the dimension of the domain.
study.la_transformations.pitfalls: Forgetting that the matrix of a map depends on both bases, and mixing the order in a composition: $ST$ means first $T$, then $S$, so the matrix product is $[S][T]$.
study.la_transformations.key_idea.0: Linearity is additivity plus homogeneity; it is enough to know the images of a basis.
study.la_transformations.key_idea.1: The columns of the matrix of $T$ are the images of the basis vectors, written in the target basis.
study.la_transformations.key_idea.2: Composition of maps corresponds to multiplication of matrices, and the identity map gives the identity matrix.
study.la_transformations.key_idea.3: A change of basis replaces $A$ by $P^{-1}AP$; similar matrices describe the same map.
study.la_transformations.theory.0: A linear transformation $T:V\to W$ satisfies $T(\alpha u+v)=\alpha T(u)+T(v)$ for all vectors and scalars. Equivalently, $T$ preserves sums and scalar multiples.
study.la_transformations.theory.1: Fix a basis $B$ of $V$ and a basis $C$ of $W$. The matrix $[T]_B^C$ has as its $j$-th column the coordinates of $T(b_j)$ in $C$. Then $[T(v)]_C=[T]_B^C[v]_B$.
study.la_transformations.theory.2: Composition is multiplication: if $T:U\to V$ and $S:V\to W$ then $[S\circ T]=[S][T]$ in matching bases. Inverses correspond as well, so $T$ is invertible exactly when its matrix is.
study.la_transformations.theory.3: A change of basis multiplies by $P^{-1}$ on one side and $P$ on the other: $B=P^{-1}AP$. The trace, the determinant and the eigenvalues are unchanged, because they belong to the map, not to the coordinates.
study.la_transformations.theory.4: Theorem (rank–nullity). For a linear map on a finite-dimensional space, $\dim V=\operatorname{rank}T+\dim\ker T$. The kernel measures the collapse, and the rank measures what survives.
study.la_transformations.example.0.probl: Write the matrix of $T(x,y)=(x+y,x-y)$ and find its kernel.
study.la_transformations.example.1.answe: $B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-4\\3&7\end{pmatrix}$, with the same trace $5$ and determinant $-2$.
study.la_determinants.title: Determinants and the characteristic polynomial
study.la_determinants.subtitle: One alternating multilinear function, and the polynomial that carries the eigenvalues.
study.la_determinants.short_answer: The determinant is the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns with $\det I=1$. It multiplies under products, it vanishes exactly for singular matrices, and its characteristic polynomial $\det(xI-A)$ has the eigenvalues as roots.
study.la_determinants.pitfalls: Adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the determinant alone, but swapping two rows changes its sign and scaling a row scales it. Dropping that sign is the most common arithmetic error.
study.la_determinants.key_idea.0: Multilinearity plus alternation plus $\det I=1$ defines the determinant uniquely.
study.la_determinants.key_idea.1: $\det(AB)=\det A\,\det B$, so a product is invertible exactly when both factors are.
study.la_determinants.key_idea.2: Cofactor expansion computes the determinant recursively along any row or column.
study.la_determinants.key_idea.3: Cayley–Hamilton: every matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.
study.la_determinants.theory.0: The determinant is the function on square matrices that is linear in each column, changes sign when two columns are swapped, and equals $1$ on the identity. These three properties force the Leibniz formula $\det A=\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i a_{i\sigma(i)}$.
study.la_determinants.theory.1: Cofactor expansion along row $i$ gives $\det A=\sum_j(-1)^{i+j}a_{ij}M_{ij}$, where $M_{ij}$ is the minor obtained by deleting row $i$ and column $j$. It is the practical way to compute a small determinant by hand.
study.la_determinants.theory.2: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero, and $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$. Determinants therefore detect singularity, but they are a poor numerical test: they can underflow or overflow long before the matrix is close to singular.
study.la_determinants.theory.3: The characteristic polynomial is $p(x)=\det(xI-A)$. Its degree is $n$, its roots are the eigenvalues, and the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ is $-\operatorname{tr}A$ while the constant term is $(-1)^n\det A$.
study.la_determinants.theory.4: Theorem (Cayley–Hamilton). $p(A)=0$ for every square matrix. This gives a way to write high powers of $A$ as combinations of lower ones, and it is the starting point of the minimal polynomial.
study.la_determinants.example.1.problem: Find the characteristic polynomial of $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and verify Cayley–Hamilton.
study.la_canonical.title: Rational and Jordan forms
study.la_canonical.subtitle: What is left of a matrix when only the map matters.
study.la_canonical.short_answer: Every matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial, and the smallest such polynomial is the minimal polynomial. It decides diagonalizability: the matrix is diagonalizable exactly when the minimal polynomial has distinct linear factors.
study.la_canonical.pitfalls: Confusing algebraic multiplicity with geometric multiplicity. A repeated eigenvalue does not by itself prevent diagonalization; too few eigenvectors does.
study.la_canonical.key_idea.0: The minimal polynomial is the monic polynomial of least degree that annihilates the matrix.
study.la_canonical.key_idea.1: A matrix is diagonalizable exactly when its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors.
study.la_canonical.key_idea.2: The Jordan form exists over $\mathbb{C}$ and collects one block per eigenvector chain.
study.la_canonical.key_idea.3: The size of the largest Jordan block for $\lambda$ is the power of $(x-\lambda)$ in the minimal polynomial.
study.la_canonical.theory.0: An annihilating polynomial of $A$ is a polynomial $p$ with $p(A)=0$. The set of annihilating polynomials is an ideal of $F[x]$, and over a field every ideal is principal, so there is a unique monic generator: the minimal polynomial.
study.la_canonical.theory.1: The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial, by Cayley–Hamilton. They share the same roots, so every eigenvalue appears in both; only the multiplicities differ.
study.la_canonical.theory.2: Diagonalizability criterion. $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix exactly when its minimal polynomial has no repeated factor, that is, when it is a product of distinct linear factors over the field.
study.la_canonical.theory.3: Over $\mathbb{C}$ every matrix is similar to a Jordan form: blocks $J_k(\lambda)$ with $\lambda$ on the diagonal and $1$ on the superdiagonal. The number of blocks for $\lambda$ is the geometric multiplicity, and the largest block size is the exponent in the minimal polynomial.
study.la_canonical.theory.4: The rational canonical form works over any field and uses companion matrices of the invariant factors instead of eigenvalues. It is the version that survives when the characteristic polynomial does not split.
study.la_canonical.example.0.problem: Find the Jordan form and minimal polynomial of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
study.la_canonical.example.1.answer: One block $J_2(2)$ and one block $J_1(3)$; the minimal polynomial is $(x-2)^2(x-3)$.
study.la_inner_products.title: Inner products and the spectral theorem
study.la_inner_products.subtitle: Length, angle, orthogonality, and why symmetric matrices are the well-behaved ones.
study.la_inner_products.short_answer: An inner product gives length and angle. Orthonormal bases make coordinates cheap, and the spectral theorem says a self-adjoint operator has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis.
study.la_inner_products.pitfalls: Normalizing at the wrong moment in Gram–Schmidt. Orthogonalize first, then divide by the norm; normalizing early makes every later projection a mess of square roots.
study.la_inner_products.key_idea.0: An inner product is bilinear, symmetric and positive definite.
study.la_inner_products.key_idea.1: Cauchy–Schwarz: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$, with equality exactly when the vectors are dependent.
study.la_inner_products.key_idea.2: Gram–Schmidt turns any independent set into an orthonormal one without changing the span.
study.la_inner_products.key_idea.3: The spectral theorem: a real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis, so $A=Q\Lambda Q^T$.
study.la_inner_products.key_idea.4: Positive definiteness is equivalent to all eigenvalues being positive, and then $A=LL^T$ with $L$ lower triangular.
study.la_inner_products.theory.0: An inner product on a real vector space is a map $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ that is linear in each argument, symmetric, and positive definite: $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for $v\ne0$. It defines $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$.
study.la_inner_products.theory.1: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\|v\|$, which is what makes angle and distance behave. It also proves the triangle inequality.
study.la_inner_products.theory.2: An orthonormal basis has $\langle q_i,q_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$. In such a basis coordinates are inner products, $c_i=\langle v,q_i\rangle$, and the matrix of a map is $Q^TAQ$.
study.la_inner_products.theory.3: Theorem (spectral). If $A$ is real and symmetric, its eigenvalues are real and eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Choosing an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors gives $A=Q\Lambda Q^T$.
study.la_inner_products.theory.4: For a general matrix the right decomposition is the SVD, $A=U\Sigma V^T$: orthonormal bases on both sides and nonnegative singular values in between. It exists for every matrix, square or not.

linalg.home.subtitle: Matrices, vector spaces, orthogonality, eigenvalues, numerics and games.
linalg.home.intro: Start with a shelf, not a tool. Each shelf is one chapter: the matrix core first, then spaces and bases, then orthogonality, eigenvalues and the factorizations they unlock. The numerical shelf follows the same ideas with floating point and iterations, and the article shelf holds the definitions and theorems behind all of it.
step.note.write_the_matrix: Write the matrix exactly as given. Every row operation below acts on these rows, so this is the object the rest of the solution works with.
step.note.write_the_vectors: List the vectors as columns. The next steps ask about their span, so only the set matters, not the order.
step.note.write_the_basis: Write the basis in a fixed order. Coordinates are read against exactly this ordered basis.
step.note.write_the_augmented_matrix: Attach the right-hand side as an extra column, so row operations carry the equations along with the coefficients.
step.note.write_the_problem: Restate the problem in symbols first, so every later step can be checked against this line.
step.note.write_the_solution: Write the answer in the variables of the original problem, not in the auxiliary ones used on the way.
step.note.eliminate: Add a multiple of one row to another. The operation is invertible, so the matrix changes but its solution set does not.
step.note.row_reduce: Continue to reduced row echelon form. There each pivot is 1 and every other entry of a pivot column is 0, so the equations can be read off directly.
step.note.back_substitution: In echelon form the last equation involves the fewest unknowns. Solve upward, and each step determines one more variable.
step.note.free_variables: Columns without a pivot are free. Setting them to parameters determines the remaining variables, which is why they generate the null space.
step.note.identify_the_pivots: The pivot columns are the ones with a leading 1. They mark the basic variables and the independent directions.
step.note.read_the_rank: The rank is the number of pivots. It is also the dimension of the column space and of the row space.
step.note.find_the_null_space: Solve $Ax=0$. Each free variable contributes one basis vector, so the nullity equals the number of non-pivot columns.
step.note.find_the_column_space: Take the pivot columns of the original matrix, not of the reduced one. Those columns are independent and span the column space.
step.note.find_the_row_space: The nonzero rows of the reduced matrix are independent and span the same row space as the original rows.
step.note.find_the_left_null_space: Solve $A^{T}y=0$. Such a $y$ is orthogonal to every column of $A$, so these vectors describe the orthogonal complement of the column space.
step.note.check_the_dimension_theorem: Rank plus nullity must equal the number of columns. This line checks the two dimensions just computed.
step.note.compute_the_determinant: Expand along a row or column, or multiply the pivots. The determinant is zero exactly when the matrix is singular.
step.note.invert_the_matrix: Row reduce $[A\mid I]$. If $A$ is invertible, the left block becomes $I$ and the right block becomes $A^{-1}$.
step.note.augment_with_the_identity: Put the identity beside the matrix. Whatever the row operations do to the left block, they also do to the right block.
step.note.find_the_cofactors: Each cofactor is a signed minor. The signs alternate like a checkerboard, starting with $+$ at the top-left entry.
step.note.apply_cramers_rule: Replace one column by the right-hand side and take determinants. The ratio gives that unknown.
step.note.build_l_and_u: Collect the multipliers into $L$ and the eliminated matrix into $U$, so that $A=LU$, or $PA=LU$ if rows were swapped.
step.note.choose_the_pivot: Pick a nonzero entry in the current column and move it into the pivot position. A zero pivot would stop the elimination.
step.note.multiply_the_matrix: Multiply row by column. Each entry is the dot product of a row of the left factor with a column of the right factor.
step.note.exponentiate_the_diagonal: A power of a diagonal matrix raises each diagonal entry to that power. The off-diagonal entries stay zero.
step.note.use_the_diagonalization: Substitute $A=PDP^{-1}$. Then powers of $A$ collapse to powers of the diagonal matrix $D$.
step.note.build_the_diagonal_factorizati: Write $A=PDP^{-1}$, with the eigenvectors as the columns of $P$ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$.
step.note.build_the_orthogonal_diagonali: A symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis, so $A=Q\Lambda Q^{T}$ and $Q^{-1}=Q^{T}$.
step.note.find_the_eigenvalues: Solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. The roots are the eigenvalues, and their multiplicities are the algebraic multiplicities.
step.note.find_the_eigenvectors: For each eigenvalue solve $(A-\lambda I)v=0$. The nonzero solutions are the eigenvectors of that eigenvalue.
step.note.build_the_characteristic_polyn: Expand $\det(A-\lambda I)$. Its degree is the size of the matrix and its roots are the eigenvalues.
step.note.compute_trace_and_determinant: The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant is their product. Both are unchanged by a change of basis.
step.note.orthogonalize_each_vector: Subtract from each vector its projection on the vectors already built. The remainder is orthogonal to all of them.
step.note.normalize_the_basis: Divide each orthogonal vector by its length. The directions stay the same and every vector now has length one.
step.note.build_q_and_r: Put the orthonormal vectors in $Q$ and the projection coefficients in $R$, so that $A=QR$ with $Q^{T}Q=I$.
step.note.build_the_normal_equations: Multiply $Ax=b$ by $A^{T}$. At the least-squares solution the residual is orthogonal to the column space, and this product expresses that condition.
step.note.solve_the_normal_equations: Solve $A^{T}A\,x=A^{T}b$. With independent columns the matrix $A^{T}A$ is invertible, so the answer is unique.
step.note.compute_the_projection: Project $b$ onto the column space. The projection is the closest point of that subspace to $b$.
step.note.compute_the_residual: The residual $b-Ax$ measures the distance from the answer to the data. At the least-squares solution it is orthogonal to the column space.
step.note.compute_the_norms: The norms give the size of the vector and of the residual, so the error can be judged without printing every entry.
step.note.compute_the_condition_number: The condition number bounds how much a relative error in the data can grow in the solution.
step.note.compute_the_leading_minors: A symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when every leading principal minor is positive.
step.note.build_cholesky: Factor $A=LL^{T}$ with $L$ lower triangular. Such a factor exists exactly when $A$ is positive definite.
step.note.compute_the_singular_values: The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{T}A$. They measure the stretch along the principal directions.
step.note.build_u_and_v: The right singular vectors are eigenvectors of $A^{T}A$; the left ones follow from $Av=\sigma u$.
step.note.compute_the_pseudoinverse: Invert the nonzero singular values and keep the orthogonal frames. This gives the least-squares inverse even when $A$ is not square.
step.note.build_the_gram_matrix: The Gram matrix collects all pairwise inner products. Its entries decide lengths, angles and independence.
step.note.build_the_transition_matrix: Express each new basis vector in the old basis. Those coordinate vectors are the columns of the transition matrix.
step.note.read_the_coordinates: The coefficients that express $v$ in the basis are its coordinates. They are unique because the basis is independent.
step.note.describe_the_subspace: Collect the conditions that every vector of the subspace satisfies. Together they describe the subspace without listing vectors.
step.note.show_closure_under_addition: Check that the sum of two members is still a member. This is the first half of the subspace test.
step.note.show_closure_under_scalar_mult: Check that a scalar multiple of a member is still a member. This is the second half of the subspace test.
step.note.show_the_zero_vector: The zero vector must belong to the set. A subset without it cannot be a subspace.
step.note.decide_independence: If the only solution of $c_1v_1+\dots+c_mv_m=0$ is the trivial one, the vectors are independent.
step.note.find_a_dependence_relation: A free variable gives a nonzero combination that equals zero, which is exactly a dependence among the vectors.
step.note.extract_a_basis: Keep the pivot columns and drop the rest. What remains is independent and spans the same space.
step.note.decide_membership: The target lies in the span exactly when the augmented system is consistent, that is, when no pivot appears in the last column.
step.note.solve_for_the_coefficients: Read the coefficients of the combination from the reduced augmented matrix.
step.note.build_the_column_matrix: Use the vectors as columns, so that a combination of them becomes a matrix-vector product.
step.note.augment_with_the_target: Put the target beside the matrix. A pivot in the target column would mean the system has no solution.
step.note.read_the_optimum: Read the optimal value from the objective row and the variable values from the final tableau.
step.note.build_the_tableau: Write the constraints and the objective in one table, so a single pivot updates all of them together.
step.note.find_the_saddle_point: A saddle point is a pair of strategies where neither player gains by changing only their own choice.
step.note.solve_the_mixed_game: Equalise the expected payoffs of the two pure strategies. The resulting probabilities make the opponent indifferent.
step.note.build_the_dft_matrix: Column $k$ of the DFT matrix holds the powers of the $k$-th root of unity, so multiplying by it evaluates the transform.
step.note.qr_iteration: Factor $A=QR$ and multiply back as $RQ$. Repeating this pushes the off-diagonal entries to zero and the diagonal to the eigenvalues.
step.note.iterate: Repeat the same update until the change falls below the tolerance. The last iterate is the reported answer.
step.note.evaluate: Substitute the current values into the expression and compute the number.
step.note.numeric_value: This is the numerical value of the expression above, rounded for display; the exact form is kept for later steps.
step.note.replace_column: Swap one column for the right-hand side and leave the rest of the determinant expansion unchanged.
